A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the political priority for newborns in Bolivia has been driven by the interaction of political commitments to development goals, the composition of the health policy network, the status of that network and political transitions and political instability.

political priority for newborn mortality reduction in Bolivia emerged on the policy and political agenda in the mid 1990s, grew through 2005 in relationship to political commitment to international development goals (MDGs and the Health for All strategy) and the support of an influential policy network, and declined later in the 2000's.
the study provides a framework for understanding the emergence and decline of political priorities for global health issues, which is a significant gap in global health policy research.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sustainability of political priority for health policy is an understudied phenomenon in the health policy literature.

the political priority of newborn survival in the 2000's in Bolivia was shaped by the interplay of a strong policy community and political commitments, which were undermined by political transition and instability.

the sustainability of newborn policy in Bolivia is uncertain and will depend on the ability of the policy network to maintain its cohesion and status, and to continue to secure the support of key actors.
